body: A drop this deep, alongside the first easing in input cost inflation for months, weakens the case for further Australian monetary tightening. That leaves the Australian dollar exposed if rate markets start pricing a gentler path. The sharp fall in new export orders also points to softening external demand, at a time when global equities are already under heavy pressure. Prices are still running above their long-run averages, though, so policymakers are unlikely to move quickly to declare inflation beaten. Traders may also treat the flash reading cautiously until the final data in early December. --- Higher interest rates are now hitting Australian demand across the board: services have joined manufacturing in contraction, new orders are at a five-year low and confidence is draining away. Australia's private sector shrank at its fastest pace in more than five years in November , according to flash survey data from S&P Global, as higher interest rates and softer demand at home and abroad hit both manufacturers and service providers. The flash composite output index fell to 46.1 from 48.2 in October. That is its lowest reading since August 2021 and the second straight month below the 50 mark that separates growth from contraction. The weakness was broad. The services business activity index dropped to 46.2 from 48.5, while the manufacturing PMI slipped to 48.7 from 49.6 and the manufacturing output index fell to 45.3 from 46.2. Services output declined at the sharpest rate in 36 months, and manufacturing output at the steepest in 25 months. Weak demand was the main driver. Total new orders fell for the first time in five months and at the fastest pace since August 2021, and services new business is now shrinking faster than manufacturing orders. Firms cited subdued economic conditions, tight budgets and higher borrowing costs. New export orders also fell at the sharpest rate in just over two years, as uncertainty in overseas markets weighed on foreign demand. With less new work coming in, businesses reduced their backlogs for the first time since June and cut staff for the second time in three months. Manufacturers shed jobs faster than service firms. Business confidence fell to a three-year low. There was some relief on prices. Input cost inflation eased for the first time in four months, even with higher fuel, transport, supplier and wage costs and a further marked lengthening of manufacturers' delivery times. Firms also raised their selling prices more slowly than in October. Both measures remain above their long-run averages. Jingyi Pan, economics associate director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said the easing in price pressures showed that the recent tightening in financial conditions was working. She cautioned, though, that falling employment and confidence point to weaker output ahead, while inflation has yet to be fully brought under control. Final November readings are due on 1 December for manufacturing and 3 December for services and the composite. Your market education doesn't end here. body: Thanksgiving Gas Prices Could Break a Record Despite Recent Plunge Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. Oil prices have traded in a narrow range over the past few sessions as forecasts of a coming surplus collide with continued attacks and stalled diplomacy in the Middle East. A run of agency reports this month has pushed expectations toward oversupply and weighed on crude. Brent crude was up 1.1% at $92.88 per barrel at 11:50 a.m. ET on Thursday, well below its October levels above 110 dollars but little changed from the start of the week, while WTI crude gained 1.7% to 84.69 dollars per barrel. The International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its November Oil Market Report that the global oil market will return to surplus in the fourth quarter as Gulf exports recover faster than global demand. Global oil supply rose to 105.4 million barrels per day in October, and the agency now sees supply exceeding demand by 1.7 million bpd in Q4 2026, a swing from its previous forecast of a 1.8 million bpd deficit. The IEA raised its Q4 supply estimate by 3.3 million bpd from last month, cut its 2027 demand forecast by 80,000 bpd to 104.3 million bpd, and lowered the implied call on OPEC crude by 220,000 bpd to 20.8 million bpd. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) has moved in the same direction . In October, it forecast a 700,000 bpd inventory draw in the fourth quarter. It now expects stocks to build in Q4 and to rise by an average of 3.5 million bpd in the first half of 2027, after drawing down for most of this year. The EIA estimates that crude production shut in across the Gulf fell to 2.5 million bpd in October, from 4.8 million bpd in September and a peak of 10.9 million bpd in May. OPEC said crude output from the OPEC+ alliance rose by roughly 2 million bpd in October, led by Saudi Arabia and Iraq. Related: Thanksgiving Gas Prices Could Break a Record Despite Recent Plunge Analysts at Standard Chartered caution that higher Gulf output does not yet mean more oil reaching buyers. Tanker shortages, damaged infrastructure and record freight rates are still holding back shipments, and inventories drained earlier this year have left little cushion. The bank also warns that the IEA’s surplus call is larger than any other agency’s, and that forecast surpluses in the past have often failed to arrive on schedule. The agencies also disagree on demand. OPEC’s November report puts global oil demand at 108.3 million bpd in 2027, almost 4 million bpd above the IEA’s figure, and keeps its forecast for 2027 demand growth at 2.55 million bpd. The two agencies measure liquids differently, so the gap overstates the disagreement, but it remains wide. The IEA expects petrochemical feedstocks to drive most of next year’s growth, with little increase in gasoline and diesel use. The EIA expects global liquids demand to grow by 2 million bpd in 2027 after falling by about the same amount this year. Standard Chartered says the demand question will decide how much of the returning Gulf supply the market can absorb. OPEC’s higher consumption forecast leaves room for far more barrels than the IEA’s. The bank expects continued attacks on shipping, maritime security risks and stalled talks to keep a geopolitical premium in prices and sustain volatility, but still sees crude prices falling through 2027 as the market slowly normalizes. In natural gas, Standard Chartered expects European prices to hold at elevated levels through winter, even if milder weather on the continent and better LNG supply bring short-term relief. Europe has already drawn heavily on storage that started the season low: EU gas inventories stood at 70.4% on Nov. 15, about 18 percentage points below the five-year average. Qatar’s LNG exports roughly doubled in October from September but remain about two-thirds below their pre-war level, and QatarEnergy’s force majeure on European deliveries runs through December. Over the past decade, the U.S. toppled Qatar and Australia…
body: Thanksgiving Gas Prices Could Break a Record Despite Recent Plunge What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… Rising U.S. oil and gas production and export capacity, along with a shift in global energy trade flows from the war in Iran, helped the United States hit record highs in crude, fuels, and LNG exports this year. In the decade since 2016, when LNG exports began, and crude oil shipments were allowed to go not only in Canada, U.S. energy exports have soared to make America one of the major crude oil exporters and the world’s biggest exporter of LNG, propane, and ethane. Over the past decade, the U.S. toppled Qatar and Australia to become the single largest LNG exporter, while it regularly exports more crude oil volumes than any of the OPEC producers except Saudi Arabia. The U.S. energy industry has beaten all oil and gas export records this year, as domestic production and capacity keep rising while supply from the Middle East collapsed in the wake of the Iran war. U.S. export volumes will continue rising in the coming years as LNG capacity expands, oil production hits record highs, and buyers prefer supply that doesn’t need to transit geopolitically sensitive chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz or the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Middle East. Related: U.S. Oil Drillers Pick Up the Pace Just as Oil Prices Fall But raising the market share would be more difficult to achieve, following a surge from a low base in the past decade that has made the U.S. a dominant supplier of LNG, oil, and fuels. Now the U.S. is competing with the top exporters of almost every major energy commodity, and further gains in market share will depend on demand and pricing, not only on geopolitical considerations. Since 2018, U.S. crude oil exports have jumped from up to 5% of global exports to up to 15% of total shipments, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters columnist Gavin Maguire. In the LNG market, the U.S. has toppled Qatar and Australia from the top spots and is now the single largest exporter with a 30% global market share in recent months, up from just 5% in 2018. In the propane market, the U.S. dominates global exports with a record market share of 70% year to date, according to Kpler’s data crunched by Reuters. U.S. propane exports increased to 2 million barrels per day (bpd) in the first half of 2026, up by 11% from a year earlier, as the Iran war crippled the Middle East’s supply to India and other countries in South Asia, EIA data showed. But continued growth in propane exports could be constrained by export capacity limitations and drought conditions at the Panama Canal related to El Niño, the U.S. administration said last month. U.S. ethane exports hit a record high of 794,000 bpd in August, the latest available EIA dataset shows . Crude oil and petroleum product exports also hit all-time highs this year, as disruptions to international crude oil and refined product flows through the Strait of Hormuz increased global demand for U.S. exports. Energy exports are further set to increase in absolute volumes, but this may not translate into gains in market share as rival exporters are also raising capacities, and those hit by the Middle East crisis are adapting to what could be lasting changes in global energy trade flows. In the oil market, the OPEC+ group is not the only competitor. Soaring production from South America’s major producers Brazil and Guyana, and Canada’s plan to build a new oil pipeline to boost sales to Asia and diversify away from the U.S., will compete with the United States for supply that’s not constrained by the Strait of Hormuz or other Middle Eastern conflicts that may arise in the future. body: West Texas Intermediate (WTI), the US crude oil benchmark, is trading around $82.80 during the Asian trading hours on Monday. WTI falls as traders weighed signs of robust crude exports against the prospect of escalating hostilities in the Middle East. The International Energy Agency (IEA) forecast a global oil surplus of roughly 2 million barrels per day (bpd) in the fourth quarter (Q4), reflecting a recovery in Middle Eastern exports that has outpaced softer demand. Additionally, Goldman Sachs Group Inc. flagged the risk of a glut next year. The robust supply outlook could undermine the WTI price in the near term. However, escalating tensions in the Middle East might cap the black gold ’s downside. Bloomberg reported over the weekend that Iran again attacked Bahrain, while Tehran-backed Houthi militants continued targeting Saudi Arabia, including the capital Riyadh. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) also reported that two tankers near Oman were struck by unidentified projectiles on Saturday. US President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post that the Islamic Republic fired more missiles and drones last week than at any time in more than a year. Trump further stated that he was inclined to resume attacks on Iran after the New Year if negotiations failed to produce an agreement. On the downside, the immediate focus is whether $82.75 can hold as a short-term pivot; a sustained break lower would open the way toward the lower Bollinger band support around $76.35, exposing a broader corrective extension. (The technical analysis of this story was written with the help of an AI tool. Know more. ) WTI Oil is a type of Crude Oil sold on international markets. The WTI stands for West Texas Intermediate, one of three major types including Brent and Dubai Crude. WTI is also referred to as “light” and “sweet” because of its relatively low gravity and sulfur content respectively. It is considered a high quality Oil that is easily refined. It is sourced in the United States and distributed via the Cushing hub, which is considered “The Pipeline Crossroads of the World”. It is a benchmark for the Oil market and WTI price is frequently quoted in the media. Like all assets, supply and demand are the key drivers of WTI Oil price. As such, global growth can be a driver of increased demand and vice versa for weak global growth. Political instability, wars, and sanctions can disrupt supply and impact prices. The decisions of OPEC, a group of major Oil-producing countries, is another key driver of price. title: Oil Price Forecast: Why Goldman Sees $150 Diesel Even As Crude Gets Cheaper - Exchange Rates UK
body: A barrel of low-sulphur diesel cost about $171 in New York Harbor on Thursday, when Brent crude traded at $95.17. Goldman Sachs expects both to get cheaper in 2027, but its forecasts still leave a wide gap. The bank puts US wholesale diesel at $150 a barrel on average, against $88 for Brent and $78 for West Texas Intermediate. The difference is already visible in what leaves the export terminals. In mid-November, Goldman estimated that global crude exports were running 12% above their 2025 average. Shipments of refined products were still 6% below theirs. “Supply adaptation is more challenging and costlier for refined products than for crude,” Goldman’s analysts wrote. Saudi Arabia can pipe crude west to its Red Sea port of Yanbu and load tankers there. A pipeline does little for a buyer who needs diesel from a damaged refinery. Goldman expects global refining capacity to grow by just 400,000 barrels a day next year. Western refiners also postponed maintenance this autumn, leaving more work for next spring, when some Middle Eastern plants may still be running below capacity. US stocks show how differently the fuel markets have responded. Distillate inventories, which include diesel and heating oil, rose by 1.6 million barrels to 104.9 million in the week to 13 November. Even with refineries operating at 95.7% of capacity, stocks remained 7% below their five-year seasonal average. Petrol inventories were 3% above theirs, according to the US Energy Information Administration . The Gulf Coast’s combined 3-2-1 refining margin has narrowed. Measured against WTI crude, it fell from about $50 a barrel on 30 October to $35 on 17 November. That calculation compares the value of two barrels of petrol and one of diesel with the cost of three barrels of crude. Cheaper petrol alone can narrow the margin while diesel buyers continue to pay a premium. For October to December 2027, Goldman forecasts Brent at $80 a barrel on average. Bank of America puts the same quarter at $74 and UBS Research at $75. The forecasts agree on cheaper crude. How much of that saving reaches diesel buyers depends on how quickly refiners can increase output. The US, China and Russia said at the 19 November summit in Shenzhen that they planned to produce and supply more refined fuel. They gave no volumes or delivery dates. For diesel buyers, the first evidence of relief would be more cargoes leaving refineries and a sustained recovery in distillate stocks. title: Oil, natural gas slip as gold jumps over 1.5% in Monday trade - Gulf News
body: Gold surges as oil and natural gas prices tumble in mixed Monday trading Commodity prices were mixed on Monday, November 23, amid an extended a three-week losing streak, while and precious metals higher, based on Trading Economics prices as of 11am in Singapore. WTI Crude oil in the US dropped 40 cents to $83.007 per barrel while Brent dropped 60 cents to $91.963 per barrel. Oil prices fell on Monday amid a "selloff" in wider financial markets, driven by concerns over whether the AI sector can boost economic growth, spilled over into commodities. Asian equities opened lower on Monday (Nov. 23), including a 4% drop in South Korea. Continuing attacks on Gulf shipping limited the losses, and Brent fell 4% last week and WTI 5%. Natural gas: Trading Economics also showed natural gas down about 4%, though it was still up 8.33% over the past month. I found no specific reason for the drop. Gold: Reports show gold futures up between about 2% and 3% in recent sessions. I found no clear driver beyond the broader market selloff. Iran: One analyst noted that oil moved lower as Trump signaled there’s no rush on an Iran decision. Over the past month, crude has fallen 18.31%, but it’s still 41.28% above a year ago. The US Energy Information Administration’s (EIA) November outlook expected Brent to stay near $100 a barrel for the rest of the year, well above the 91.963 on your screen. The outlook says oil rose for a third consecutive month in October, citing tanker attacks in the Persian Gulf, tighter supply and higher shipping costs. Watch for any decision from Washington, further tanker attacks and a possible equity rebound. I couldn’t find reasons for the moves in wheat, soybeans, copper and coal. US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has claimed that the sharp decline in oil prices following the November midterm elections vindicates his earlier predictions, describing the controversy surrounding energy prices as a “Giant Hoax”. In a social media post on Monday, November 23, Trump questioned the timing of the decline in oil prices, suggesting that the movement had happened as he had anticipated. “Isn’t it interesting that Oil prices have dropped precipitously after the Midterm Elections? I said that was going to happen,” Trump wrote. Trump's remarks appear aimed at countering criticism over energy costs, particularly the impact of oil and fuel prices on American households, businesses and the wider economy. Oil prices are politically sensitive in the US because changes in crude prices can influence gasoline, diesel, transportation and food costs. Energy prices also affect inflation expectations and consumer confidence, making them an important issue for voters. However, a decline in oil prices following an election does not, by itself, establish that the election caused the movement or that political predictions were responsible. Global crude prices are influenced by several factors, including supply and demand, OPEC+ production decisions, geopolitical developments, inventories, currency movements and expectations about economic growth. Trump's post puts oil prices back at the centre of the political debate, as the administration seeks to highlight falling energy costs as evidence of economic progress.

title: Could Another Fed Rate Hike Be A Policy Mistake? Bill Ackman Says 3% Inflation Target Is More Realistic - TradingView
body: The Federal Reserve is set to meet in December for its last policy decision of 2026, with markets overwhelmingly expecting a rate hike after policymakers raised concerns about rising inflation. However, some Wall Street experts, including Pershing Square Inc.’s (PS) Bill Ackman, believe that a hike would be a policy mistake under current circumstances. In a post on X, the activist investor said that he thinks the central bank is “about to make another mistake on December 9th” if it hikes interest rates under massively tightening financial conditions. He noted that the cost of equity capital has increased materially, even as there has been a recent decline in the stock market. Ackman highlighted the example of SpaceX (SPCX) , saying that the investment-grade company had recently raised secured debt financing at an 8.259% interest rate versus significantly below 6% for its unsecured bond offering at the time of its IPO. He also said that the Fed’s 2% inflation ambition is misguided. “Geopolitical risk and the required investment in global military spending, de-globalization and tariffs, and the massive AI infrastructure and related energy investment are features of the world that did not exist when the 2% target was set.” As per the hedge fund manager, 3% inflation is a more realistic ambition. “The Fed will put the U.S. and world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%,” he said. In the meantime, services inflation has exceeded that rate 95% of the time over the past 60 years. “The target is not sacred. Another choice by central bankers not supported by theory or facts,” he added. Meanwhile, economist Peter Schiff posited that the Fed knows it cannot deliver the rate hikes necessary to return inflation to 2% without creating a financial crisis. “So the Fed threatens to hike, crashing stocks and commodities, which raises the odds of a recession, giving it an excuse not to hike,” he said. title: Bitcoin drops below $56,000: Why a stronger U.S. dollar matters to Somalia - Hiiraan Online
body: Mogadishu (HOL) — Bitcoin briefly fell below $56,000 on Saturday, Nov. 21, hitting its lowest level in more than two years as a stronger U.S. dollar and uncertainty over American interest rates weighed on cryptocurrency markets. The world's largest cryptocurrency dropped to approximately $55,000 before recovering toward $60,000 later in the day. The decline left Bitcoin more than 50% below its October 2025 peak of over $126,000. The more immediate concern is the strengthening U.S. dollar, which can increase the cost of sending remittances for Somali workers earning their incomes in other currencies. Bitcoin's latest decline comes amid growing uncertainty in international financial markets over U.S. interest rates, inflation and the outlook for economic growth. Investors have reassessed expectations for Federal Reserve monetary policy, contributing to a stronger dollar and increasing pressure on risk-sensitive assets, including cryptocurrencies and technology stocks. The U.S. Dollar Index, which measures the dollar against a basket of major currencies, approached 104 during the week, reportedly its highest level in approximately 19 months. A stronger dollar can make dollar-denominated investments more expensive for international investors, while expectations of higher interest rates can increase the attractiveness of cash and government bonds relative to speculative assets. Bitcoin has also faced selling pressure from institutional investors, including funds holding the cryptocurrency through exchange-traded products. Institutional selling, combined with the forced liquidation of leveraged trading positions, has contributed to sharp price movements. The latest selloff highlights Bitcoin's continued vulnerability to changes in global financial conditions, despite its frequent promotion as a digital alternative to traditional stores of value. Somalia is among the economies most dependent on remittances from citizens living and working abroad. According to the Central Bank of Somalia's 2025 annual report, individual remittances reached $3.13 billion, up from $2.72 billion in 2024. These transfers represented approximately 24% of Somalia's gross domestic product in 2025, demonstrating their importance to household consumption and economic stability. Remittances help families pay for food, housing, education, healthcare and other basic necessities. Unlike countries where households primarily use domestic currencies, Somalia's economy is heavily dollarized. Many consumers receive, store and spend U.S. dollars through mobile money platforms such as EVC Plus, Zaad and Sahal. This system means changes in the dollar's international value can directly affect the cost of remittances for Somali workers living abroad. For example, a Somali worker in London earning British pounds must convert those earnings into U.S. dollars before sending money home. If the pound falls from $1.35 to $1.31, sending $200 would cost approximately £153 instead of £148, excluding transfer fees. The difference may appear modest for a single transaction, but repeated monthly transfers can become more expensive for workers supporting relatives in Somalia. The same pressure affects Somali workers earning euros, Canadian dollars and other currencies that weaken against the U.S. dollar. A stronger dollar does not necessarily reduce the amount received by a family in Somalia if the sender continues transferring the same dollar amount. Instead, it increases the cost for senders earning weaker foreign currencies. Somalia's reliance on the U.S. dollar provides some protection against exchange-rate instability compared with economies that depend on rapidly depreciating domestic currencies. However, dollarization does not shield households from inflation or increases in international commodity prices. Federal Reserve officials are weighing whether to raise interest rates by a quarter-point or a half-point at the December 8-9 meeting, now less than three weeks away. Chairman Kevin Warsh has mostly stopped offering clues about coming decisions, leaving colleagues to state their preferences publicly. The Fed is raising rates to cool inflation that has run above its 2% target for nearly six years, and the size of the December move will shape borrowing costs across the U.S. economy. Investment in AI infrastructure is adding inflationary pressure by driving up demand for electricity, construction and specialized equipment. Growth accelerated to a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter while the unemployment rate stood at 4.1%, and October headline inflation for the Fed's preferred gauge is estimated at 3.8%. Chairman of the Federal Reserve, who has pulled back from offering forward guidance on upcoming rate decisions. Federal Reserve governor who has advocated for either a half-point December hike or a quarter-point move followed by another in January. Minutes from the Fed's October meeting showed that almost all officials expected additional rate increases would be appropriate. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee declined to rule out a larger increase, while Fed governor Christopher Waller has advocated either a half-point move in December or a quarter-point move with a clear signal that another hike will follow in January. The December decision extends a tightening cycle that began in 2022, when the Fed started raising rates to bring inflation down from multi-decade highs. A quarter-point increase would push the target federal funds range to 4.00%-4.25%, which feeds into the rates on mortgages, car loans and credit cards. A larger half-point move would raise those borrowing costs faster, so households carrying variable-rate debt would feel the change sooner. Micron delivered its Q2 FY2026 earnings report March 26, topping the board in virtually every respect. Revenue rose 62% YoY to $8.71B. The firm reported non-GAAP EPS of $1.85, well above the Street’s expectation. Non-GAAP gross margin expanded to 45.8%, from significantly lower levels a year earlier, due to a mix-shift to higher-value HBM and data centre DRAM at the expense of lower-margin consumer memory. Data Center revenue, which includes HBM and enterprise DRAM, grew >150% YoY, the fastest rate the company has recorded. The company also raised full-year FY2026 revenue guidance to $31.5 to $33.5B, implying sequential revenue growth for the balance of 2026. Of the many things the Q2 FY2026 earnings call told us, the most important for understanding the near-term fundamental thesis is the discussion about being sold out on HBM allocations for most of 2026. This means that Micron is unable to meet all of its demand for this memory. HBM3E, Micron’s current-gen high bandwidth memory stack, is the memory stack sitting directly atop the interposer of Nvidia’s H100, H200, and Blackwell GPUs. In other words, the memory stack is what powers the GPU. There are only 3 vendors on the planet, Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix, that can produce HBM at commercial scale. Micron’s HBM3E being sold out through much of 2026 isn’t a bad thing in that Micron is leaving money on the table. Rather, it means Micron has locked up multiyear supply contracts with major hyperscalers for contracted HBM3E pricing, which transitions the memory business away from commodity cycles, to something closer to a more visibility driven model. This would constitute a significant re-rating opportunity in the shares. Standard DRAM is, by its nature, a commodity. The per-GB price is determined by the intersection of supply and demand around the world. When there is too much supply in relation to demand (such as in CY2023/2024) then the per-GB margin shrinks to near zero. HBM, by contrast, is not a commodity. HBM manufacturing involves a unique stack-based approach that only a very few companies around the globe have mastered at commercial scales. If he comes through those interviews unscathed and makes a serious bid to return, Goldberg said the board would probably have to resist, putting interim CEO Colette Kress in an awkward spot. title: Elon Musk Says 2027 AI Cash Crunch Will Be ‘Nuts’ — Analysts Still See SpaceX Emerging As The Biggest AI Hyperscaler - Yahoo Finance
body: Musk warned that AI data center delays could create a 2027 cash gap of hundreds of billions of dollars. Dan Ives sees SpaceX becoming the biggest AI hyperscaler as demand outpaces planned capacity. Tesla cut AI4.5 memory by 25% and Musk said AI5 will go to Optimus. A day after investors lined up to finance $44 billion of AI equipment for SpaceX (SPCX), CEO Elon Musk warned that even a few months of data center delays could leave the industry needing hundreds of billions more. SPCX shares fell 8% to $127.79 on Friday, bringing their weekly decline to 8%, the steepest this month. See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox Musk warned on Saturday that AI companies could face a cash crunch in 2027 as they wait for costly chips to start earning revenue. He was responding to AI researcher Francois Chollet, who said graphics processors were scarce and getting more expensive to rent. Even after the chips arrive, Musk said, operators still have to power and cool them and get them running reliably enough to bill customers. "The cash shortage is also going to be nuts next year," Musk said. "Even cumulative industry delays of a few months between paying for compute and getting it reliable enough to generate revenue will mean hundreds of billions of incremental dollars just for working capital. Where will that come from?" "I own $SPCX and believe it may be the largest AI hyperscaler in the not too distant future," Futurum CEO Daniel Newman said. He also owns specialist cloud providers Iren (IREN) and CoreWeave (CRWV). If smaller providers struggle to finance their next data center, he said, SpaceX faces fewer rivals bidding for customers and gains more room to set prices. "The conditions Elon speaks to are real, but creating a massive spiral for smaller AI clouds is definitely in his best interest. It's good use of the platform and a good chess move. But it isn't just some altruistic advice for investors," Newman said. Iren had the funding in place and the timing still slipped. Its first Horizon data center went live for Microsoft, and quarterly AI cloud revenue nearly tripled to $200 million. But a customer's design change and suppliers' schedules pushed back Iren's target for bringing more than $4 billion in annualized contracted revenue online. The company now expects to reach that level in January, possibly as late as the end of February, after initially targeting year-end. CoreWeave, meanwhile, expects customers to help cover the wait between buying chips and earning revenue from them. Earlier this month, it said it expected about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months. On Friday, Apollo and Goldman Sachs increased a debt offering to about $44 billion after investor orders exceeded the amount available. The financing will pay for Nvidia's Vera Rubin chips and related equipment, which SpaceX expects to start leasing in the first half of 2027. SpaceX ended September with 1.7 gigawatts of rated computing capacity, and Musk said he would be surprised to finish 2027 below 13 GW. The company plans to invest more than $74 billion in computing campuses in Texas and Arizona. For one customer, full delivery triggers a $3.1 billion monthly bill. Anthropic (ANT), the Claude developer that closed its IPO at $83 a share on Friday, expects to receive all the capacity it ordered from SpaceX's AI unit in December. Spending could hit $120.5 billion through 2029, but either side can cancel with 90 days' notice after the initial contract periods end in early 2027. SpaceX (SPCX) could become the next biggest hyperscaler, according to Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives. He named Musk's company among the potential winners in the tech sell-off, pointing to demand for AI computing power that he expects will outstrip planned capacity. Ives put AI-related power demand and backlog at 160 gigawatts through 2029

title: Broadcom's December 9 Test: Can AI Demand Be Converted Into Profit? - ad-hoc-news.de
body: Broadcom shares shed 12% on Friday as a broad selloff swept through AI chip stocks, leaving the stock at €277.80 — roughly 35% below its 52-week high. The retreat came as investors began questioning both the scale and the profitability of spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure, according to Reuters, with AP reporting that chip names came under pressure on worries about AI expenditures and the pace of the infrastructure buildout. For holders of Broadcom stock, that shift in sentiment pushes a more specific question to the fore: how much profitable business can the company actually capture from all this spending? The answer will determine whether Friday's lower price marks an attractive entry point or simply reflects expectations for the AI business that have been marked down for good. Size alone doesn't settle the matter. Even if demand for AI infrastructure holds up, what counts for Broadcom is how much of that demand lands in its own order book — and how much margin comes with it. An outlook that merely points to rising demand would therefore carry less weight than one that addresses how the business tied to that demand is likely to develop. Analyst moves in the days before Friday's drop illustrate how the Street is balancing those two ideas. Goldman Sachs trimmed its price target to $460 from $540 on Wednesday while keeping its buy rating, citing lower valuation multiples among comparable companies. The firm now applies a multiple of 25 times earnings to Broadcom, down from the 30 times it had used previously. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Broadcom? TD Cowen also stayed at buy, though it lowered its target to $425 from $475. Rothschild & Co went further in the prior Friday's session, downgrading Broadcom to neutral from buy and cutting its target to $398 from $595. Buy ratings on their own, in other words, no longer signal that the houses put the same valuation on the shares as before. The more favorable scenario would see AI infrastructure investment remain substantial and Broadcom convert it into profitable growth. An outlook along those lines could ease the doubts that shaped Friday's trading. To make that case, the company need not promise any further acceleration in spending — what matters is that expected demand translates into a profitable business. The danger isn't confined to a possible slowdown in investment. Even with spending running high, Broadcom's slice of the business could prove less lucrative than anticipated. That is why the next hard data point carries weight: Broadcom has scheduled fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 results for December 9, 2026. Should AI demand continue to offer a path to profitable growth, a rebound in the share price remains plausible. If the guidance instead points to weaker demand or thinner returns from the AI business, the lower price by itself would be no argument for a recovery. Fresh Broadcom information released. title: Nasdaq Falls 10% in a Week as AI Stocks Sell Off Sharply - JournalArta
body: The Nasdaq dropped 10% this week, its worst showing since March 2020, while the S&P 500 and Dow entered corrections. Investors fear the AI trade is unraveling, and analysts doubt a quick rebound after Anthropic's debut failed to lift sentiment. US stocks suffered one of their worst weeks in years as investors questioned how much air can come out of the AI trade. The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 10% for the week, its worst result since March 2020, when pandemic lockdowns began. The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average both closed Friday in a correction, meaning a drop of 10% from their recent highs. Investors had hoped this week's stock market debut of AI company Anthropic would lift sentiment. It did not. Anthropic gained 17% on its first day, then slumped more than 8% on Friday to close near its IPO price. The selloff follows weeks of worry about whether the AI boom can last. In September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. AI firms borrow billions to build data centers, so higher rates make that more costly. Democrats also won both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections. They have vowed tougher regulation of AI and a slowdown in data center construction, which has proved unpopular with voters. At Nvidia, the top AI chip company, CEO Jensen Huang resigned this month. He had been suspected of an affair with a woman believed to have been spying for China. Nvidia still posted strong results this week. Hank Smith, head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, does not expect the quick recoveries seen after earlier AI dips. "I think it has taken the market the better part of the last two or three weeks to realize it is not going to be like the previous sell-offs," he said. He added that AI could fall "out of favor" through next year. Smith rejected comparisons with the dot-com bust of 2000. He noted that today's AI trade is driven by large firms such as Meta and Apple, which he does not see going out of business. The outlook for AI, he said, is "not based on a pie in the sky." Even so, he said it is unclear whether investors will earn the returns they expect. Another worry is how tightly AI companies are linked. Nvidia owns shares in firms such as Anthropic and lends them money, and they in turn buy its chips. It is also a major investor in CoreWeave, which borrows heavily to build data centers. Some fear that trouble at one or two companies could set off a chain reaction and a wider financial crisis. The US economy leans heavily on AI. Investment in the sector helped the economy grow at an annual rate of 3.4% in the most recent quarter. AI stocks also make up a large share of the S&P 500, so they sit inside index funds, pensions and 401(k) retirement accounts.
